title: Turn the Axes, Change Every Number
scopeNote: This keeps the live rotation over a fixed marker configuration, the recomputing loading table and the invariants that refuse to move. The second marker set, the oblique control and the closing challenge stay in the longer version. The prediction already asks the fit question the original challenge asked again at the end.
summary: Twelve markers sit fixed in the plane of a two-factor solution. Rotate the axes and every loading changes while the fit, each communality and the total variance stay exactly where they were.
learningObjectives: State what rotation changes and what it leaves untouched.
Explain why no rotation can be more correct than another in any sense the data settles.
Distinguish the variance carried by one factor, which rotation moves, from the total variance accounted for, which it does not.
Defend simple structure as a criterion researchers impose rather than a solution the data contains.
Explain why a factor label is an interpretive act, and why a cross-loading cannot be rotated away.
interactionTypes: a prediction about model fit before anything is shown
a live rotation control over a fixed configuration of markers
a loading table that recomputes at every angle
invariant readouts that visibly refuse to move
a live factor-naming sentence that changes with the angle
a guided rotation to the varimax optimum
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with rotation on a native range input reporting its angle in text. Every loading is in a real table with row and column headers, so the figure is never the only route to the numbers; the table also carries a plain-language column saying which factor each marker reads as. Markers are numbered in the figure and by the same number in the table, so no point has to be identified by colour or position alone. The chart description gives the current angle, the highest-loading marker on each factor, the variance on each factor and the invariant total. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: Twelve invented markers with illustrative coordinates. They were constructed to make rotation legible, not sampled from a dataset, and nothing here is an estimate of how any real adjectives covary.
simulationNotes: Each marker has fixed polar coordinates in the plane spanned by the two extracted factors, and rotating the axes by theta re-expresses it as r cos(phi - theta) and r sin(phi - theta). Because that is a rotation, r is fixed, so every communality is fixed and so is their sum, which is the same statement as the fit not changing. The variance carried by each factor separately does change, and it is displayed beside the total precisely because it is the moving number most easily mistaken for a change in fit. The configuration was built so that the two clusters sit ninety degrees apart, which lets an orthogonal rotation reach a clean simple structure; one marker sits between the clusters and remains a genuine cross-loading at every angle; one sits near the origin and has a low communality at every angle. At zero degrees the first factor contrasts one cluster against the other, which is what an unrotated extraction typically looks like and the reason anyone rotates. The guided button maximises the normalised varimax criterion, searched over whole degrees because the slider offers whole degrees, and lands at 47. Simplification: the axes are held at ninety degrees, so the factors cannot correlate. The caution says what oblique rotation would add and that it too leaves the fit unchanged.
readmeTopic: what rotation changes in a factor analysis, and what it cannot change
